newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN-Axa in Belgium, Lloyd's in Japan.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN-Axa in Belgium, Lloyd's in Japan.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

In 1987 Axa tried to scoop up Belgian insurer Royale Belge as part of its plan to create a major insurance group by raising its stake in the group from 10 percent to 32 percent via a series of share purchases. There was resistance from Belgian stock holders, and UAP came in as the knight in shining armour, taking a stake in the group and allowing Belgian shareholders backed by Groupe Bruxelles Lambert and Generale de Banque to form a group to resist Axa expansion. In the end GBL and UAP bought out Axa's entire stake.
How ironic it is therefore that the tables have turned, and that as a result of Axa's takeover of UAP, Royale Belge looks set to merge with Axa Belgium.
Arrangements for closer links are not likely to be finalised for several weeks. There are some sensitive problem areas to be overcome, such as existing relationships with brokers and agents.

But a merger would push the combined group ahead of Fortis and give it premium income of around Bfr86.3 billion. Both are strong in the non-life sector and both have been trying to shift their portfolios towards life insurance in search of better profits.
If the merger does go ahead, Axa will benefit from Royale Belge's experience in bancassurance. Other than increased market share, it is harder to see what the advantages would be for Royale Belge.
--oo0oo--

Lloyd's of London chairman Sir David Rowland insisted at a reception last week that the 309 year old society will still be around in another 100 years. Today he arrives in Tokyo to spread, no doubt, a similar message. In has role as chief marketing man, he will use his persuasive skills to drum-up interest in a new subsidiary, Lloyd's Japan, being opened tomorrow.

Lloyd's is looking for markets to make up n revenue it lost during its bad years. It feels it can succeed in Japan, which is now allowing brokers to trade for the first time, because it has the history, old-fashioned manners, and, dare we say, dignity that will appeal to status-conscious Japanese clients.

Rowland will tell audiences this week that the restructuring plan is going well and that there is nothing to worry about. Meanwhile, recent setbacks in its progress against U.S. litigation will be highlighted again in the UK on Friday with the start of the 'refuseniks' case - Lloyd's names who say they will not pay the cash demands made by the society because they have evidence they were recruited without being told of their exposure to asbestos and pollution-related claims.
